text: Every code in this course has been building toward one number: how many real, physical qubits does it actually take to get one qubit's worth of reliable, protected logical information? The answer depends heavily on which code family you pick.

Chapter 5 built this formula directly from the lattice geometry: a distance-d surface code uses 2 d squared minus 1 total physical qubits to protect 1 logical qubit. Verified across a wide range: distance 3 costs 17 qubits, distance 5 costs 49, distance 7 costs 97, distance 9 costs 161, distance 11 costs 241, distance 15 costs 449, distance 21 costs 881, distance 27 costs 1,457, and distance 41 costs 3,361. Increasing d buys exponentially lower logical error rates, covered next lesson, at a cost that grows only quadratically.

Contrast this against repeatedly concatenating the Steane 7-1-3 code from Chapter 4 — encoding each physical qubit of a Steane-encoded logical qubit using another Steane code, for L levels, each level multiplying the physical-qubit count by 7. Level 1 costs 7 qubits, level 2 costs 49, level 3 costs 343, level 4 costs 2,401. At low levels this looks competitive, even better, than the surface code — level 1's 7 qubits beats even the surface code's smallest useful distance of 17. But the growth is exponential in L, not quadratic, and by level 4 it already costs more than a distance-15 surface code's 449 qubits.

This is the central, honest point: at small scale, concatenation can look cheaper. At the scale real fault-tolerant algorithms actually need, the surface code's quadratic growth wins decisively, because exponential curves always eventually overtake quadratic ones, no matter how good the exponential curve's starting point looked. That — not any claim that the surface code is cheap in an absolute sense — is the real reason it's favored at scale, on top of the hardware-connectivity reasons from Chapter 5.
Next lesson covers the theoretical result that justifies all of this: the error threshold theorem, which says scaling up a code is actually worth doing, provided one condition holds.
